newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German EMU debate heats up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German EMU debate heats up.

text.p: Germany's domestic debate about European economic and monetary union (EMU), long stifled by a broad elite consensus, heated up on Friday with strong opposition to delaying the euro and calls for more flexible criteria.

Senior leaders of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and his Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners warned of dire consequences if the euro were delayed beyond 1999 because the criteria were too strictly interpreted.

But the Bavarian-based Christian Social Union (CSU) kept up the pressure on its chairman, Finance Minister Theo Waigel, for a water-tight interpretation of the three percent target for budget deficits as part of gross domestic product.

The debate, which flared up after Waigel's failed grab for Bundesbank gold and the left-wing shift in France, revealed cracks in the political elite's hitherto united pro-EMU stand which is not shared by the more sceptical voters. New opinion polls say 71 percent of Germans want EMU put off.
Heiner Geissler, deputy CDU parliamentary leader and a key voice on the party's left wing, said Bonn had set itself a trap with its "criteria fetishism" over the euro.
"I would consider it one of the worst mistakes possible to delay the euro because of the question of 3.0 percent or 3.2 percent," Geissler told German Radio.

Former foreign minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher, still an influential voice on foreign affairs and within his FDP, warned delaying EMU was a dangerous game that would lead Bonn into "ice-cold isolation."
"Whoever claims the treaty demands a pinpoint landing on a 3.0 percent target is giving Maastricht a different meaning than its text," said Genscher, who negotiated the treaty for Bonn.

Waigel, whose failed bid to force the Bundesbank to pay out profits from revalued gold stocks helped stoke the EMU debate, denied a front-page story in Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung that leaders of his CSU expected the euro to be delayed.
But one of his deputies, Bavarian state social affairs minister Barbara Stamm, said on Friday: "I cannot imagine how the criteria can still be met."
"The criteria have to be right," she said, adding the criteria determined EMU's launch, not the 1999 deadline.

Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber, a powerful Waigel rival and critic, denied the CSU was debating a delay but said European Union members were no longer in agreement about EMU's stability after the French election.
"For the CSU it has always been clear that convergence determines the schedule (for EMU) and not vice versa," he said.
In an unusual move reflecting the role the Bavarians play in influencing Bonn's EMU stand, the CSU said Waigel would defend his policies before a special party meeting on June 18.

Waigel, who set a record as Bonn's longest-serving finance minister last week after eight years, has long demanded that all EMU members meet the Maastricht deficit target and its 60 percent debt-to-GDP target precisely.
On his insistence and amid criticism from other countries, the EU approved a "stability pact" to fine EMU members that overshoot these targets once the monetary union has started.

But a shortfall of at least 19 billion marks ($11 billion) in his 1997 budget, caused mainly by high unemployment and falling tax revenues, has meant Waigel has had to grasp for new funds with what critics say is the same kind of "creative accounting" he and the Bundesbank have long condemmed.

Waigel was humiliated this week when the Bundesbank forced him to back down from a hostile plan to force the central bank to revalue its gold stocks and pay him out an extra profit to enable Bonn to meet the deficit target precisely.

Genscher also warned against overlooking the economic progress the Maastricht process had brought to countries like Italy, an EU member Bonn and the Bundesbank seem determined to leave out of the first wave of EMU participants.
"We can only speak with highest respect of the efforts made in many member states, for example Italy," he wrote.
